tagline: A valley highway links Salmon, a railroad town and charcoal kilns
intro: Idaho 28 follows the Lemhi Valley between Salmon and the highway junction near Mud Lake. Idaho designates its entire length the Sacajawea Historic Byway. Between Salmon and Leadore, the road runs beside the Lemhi River for several miles.

Sacajawea was born in the Lemhi Valley near Salmon. The Lewis and Clark Expedition crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass and followed the Salmon River through the site of the present city. A later transport connection linked the valley’s towns: from 1910 to 1939, Salmon was the western terminus of the Gilmore and Pittsburgh Railroad.

Traveling southeast from Salmon, Idaho 28 passes through Lemhi and then Leadore, where it meets Idaho 29. The highway continues toward Mud Lake and its junction with Idaho 33. Terreton lies east of Mud Lake.

moments.title: Salmon
moments.text: The Lemhi River meets the Salmon River near downtown Salmon. Sacajawea was born in the Lemhi Valley, and the city’s Sacajawea Interpretive, Cultural and Educational Center opened in August 2003. The center interprets the Salmon and Lemhi River country, including Sacajawea, her people and the Lewis and Clark Expedition. Its 71 acres adjoin the Lemhi River and include outdoor trails, community gardens and a research library. The expedition crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass, southeast of Salmon, before following the Salmon River through the present city and turning north toward Montana.

moments.title: Leadore
moments.text: Leadore’s community center is a railway-station replica, built in 2001. The town dates from 1910, when the Gilmore and Pittsburgh Railroad crossed Bannock Pass into the Lemhi Valley. The intended station site at Junction changed because its landowner refused to sell. Leadore housed the repair shops and the junction of the Gilmore branch with the main line. The railroad stopped operating in 1939. Idaho 28 now passes through town as Railroad Street. The Lemhi River crosses the northeast side of Leadore, flowing northwest to meet the Salmon River at Salmon.

moments.title: Birch Creek Charcoal Kilns
moments.text: Four kiln ruins survive from a group of sixteen built in 1886 to fuel the Nicholia smelter. Warren King built them with bricks made from local clay. Each beehive-shaped kiln measured about 20 feet tall and 20 feet across. The operation lasted less than three years. A volunteer-assisted stabilization saved one kiln from collapse in 1987, and the Forest Service restored the kilns in 2000. Nothing survives of Woodland, the nearby settlement where kiln workers lived. Each kiln consumed 30 to 40 cords of Douglas fir per load, burning for two days to produce charcoal.
